title: Quick multiplication
body: Multiplication check.
explanation: 7 × 7 = 49. A quick check: 7 × 5 = 35, plus 7 × 2 = 14, gives 49.

title: A dozen dozens
body: Squares you should know by heart.
explanation: 12 × 12 = 144, also called a gross. Check: 12 × 10 = 120, plus 12 × 2 = 24, gives 144.

title: Percent of a number
body: Mental percentages.

title: A quarter of 80
body: Mental percentages.
explanation: 25% is one quarter. 80 ÷ 4 = 20.

title: Times table check
body: Multiplication check.

title: Six sevens
body: Multiplication check.

title: Multiplying decimals
body: Half of a half.
explanation: Half of a half is a quarter: 0.5 × 0.5 = 0.25.

title: Adding fractions
body: Fractions check.
explanation: Add the tops when the bottoms match: 1/4 + 1/4 = 2/4 = 1/2. The bottom number does not change.

title: Square roots
body: Square root check.
explanation: 9 × 9 = 81, so the square root of 81 is 9.

title: Powers of two
body: Powers check.

title: Is it prime?
body: Prime number check.
explanation: 17 can only be divided exactly by 1 and 17, so it is prime.

title: A tricky prime
body: Prime number check.
explanation: 5 + 1 = 6, which divides by 3, so 51 divides by 3: 51 = 3 × 17.

title: Solve for x
body: Basic algebra.
explanation: Subtract 5 from both sides: 3x = 15. Divide by 3: x = 5.

title: Solve for x again
body: Basic algebra.
explanation: Add 4 to both sides: 2x = 14. Divide by 2: x = 7.

title: Up 10%, down 10%
body: Percentage change trap.
statement: A 10% rise then a 10% fall brings a price back to where it started
explanation: 100 up 10% is 110. 110 down 10% is 110 − 11 = 99. The fall is taken from a bigger number.

title: Triangle angles
body: Geometry check.
statement: The angles of a triangle add up to 180°
explanation: In any flat triangle the three inside angles always add up to 180°.

title: Times eleven
body: Multiplication check.
explanation: Put the sum of the digits in the middle: 1, (1 + 3), 3 gives 143.

title: Dividing by a half
body: Division trap.
explanation: Dividing by 0.5 means asking how many halves fit in 45. That is 90. Dividing by a half doubles a number.

title: Fraction to decimal
body: Fractions and decimals.

title: Finding the average
body: Mean check.
explanation: Add them: 4 + 8 + 12 = 24. Divide by how many there are: 24 ÷ 3 = 8.

title: Negative times negative
body: Signs check.
explanation: A negative times a negative is positive: (−3) × (−4) = 12.

title: Area of a square
body: Geometry check.
statement: A square with 5 cm sides has an area of 20 cm²
explanation: Area = side × side = 5 × 5 = 25 cm². 20 cm is its perimeter (4 × 5), not its area.

title: Swapping percentages
body: Percent trick.
explanation: x% of y always equals y% of x. Here both are 10.

title: Dividing by eight
body: Division check.
explanation: Halve three times: 1,000 → 500 → 250 → 125.

title: Near a hundred
body: Multiplication check.

title: Two answers
body: Algebra trap.
statement: x² = 49 has only one solution, x = 7
explanation: (−7) × (−7) is also 49, so there are two solutions: 7 and −7.

title: Order of operations
body: Brackets, powers, times and divide, plus and minus.
explanation: Multiply before adding: 3 × 4 = 12, then 2 + 12 = 14. You only get 20 with brackets: (2 + 3) × 4.

title: Multiply by 11 in your head
body: For a two-digit number, write its digits apart and put their sum in the middle. 34 × 11: 3, (3 + 4 = 7), 4 gives 374. If the sum is 10 or more, carry 1 to the left: 57 × 11 is 5, 12, 7, so 627.

title: The percentage swap trick
body: x% of y equals y% of x. Hard ones become easy: 8% of 25 is the same as 25% of 8, which is 2. And 4% of 75 is 75% of 4, which is 3.

title: Squaring numbers ending in 5
body: Take the first digit, multiply it by the next number up, then write 25 after it. 35²: 3 × 4 = 12, so 1,225. 65²: 6 × 7 = 42, so 4,225.

title: Multiply by 5 quickly
body: Multiplying by 5 is the same as multiplying by 10 and halving. 5 × 68: 680 ÷ 2 = 340. 5 × 43: 430 ÷ 2 = 215.

title: What is a prime number?
body: A prime number is a whole number greater than 1 that can only be divided exactly by 1 and itself: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13... The number 2 is the only even prime. 1 is not prime.

title: The order of operations
body: Work in this order: Brackets, then powers, then multiply and divide from left to right, then add and subtract from left to right. So 10 − 2 × 3 = 10 − 6 = 4, not 24.

title: Solving a simple equation
body: Whatever you do to one side, do to the other, until x is alone. 4x + 3 = 23: take 3 from both sides (4x = 20), then divide both sides by 4 (x = 5). Check: 4 × 5 + 3 = 23.

title: Working out a percentage change
body: Percentage change = (new − old) ÷ old × 100. A price going from 80 to 100: (100 − 80) ÷ 80 × 100 = 25% rise. Always divide by the starting value.

title: Divisible by 3 or 9?
body: Add the digits. If the sum divides by 3, the number divides by 3. If the sum divides by 9, the number divides by 9. 2,457: 2 + 4 + 5 + 7 = 18, so it divides by both 3 and 9.

title: Mean, median and mode
body: Mean: add everything and divide by the count. Median: the middle value when sorted. Mode: the most common value. For 2, 3, 3, 8, 14: mean 6, median 3, mode 3. One big value pulls the mean but not the median.

title: Estimate before you calculate
body: Round first to see the rough answer: 49 × 21 is about 50 × 20 = 1,000. The exact answer (1,029) should be close. If your calculation gives 10,290, you know something went wrong.

title: Logic: the Monty Hall puzzle
body: A prize is behind one of 3 doors. You pick one. The host, who knows, opens another door with no prize and lets you switch. Switching wins 2 times in 3, because your first pick was right only 1 time in 3.

title: Zero as a number
body: The Indian mathematician Brahmagupta wrote rules for calculating with zero, including adding and subtracting it, in 628 CE. Treating zero as a number in its own right was a huge step for mathematics.

title: Pi never ends
body: Pi (π), the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter, is about 3.14159. It is irrational: its decimals go on forever without repeating, so it can never be written exactly as a fraction.

title: The birthday paradox
body: In a room of just 23 people, there is a better than 50% chance that two of them share a birthday. It feels wrong, but there are 253 different pairs of people to compare.

title: What is a googol?
body: A googol is 1 followed by 100 zeros (10¹⁰⁰). The name was coined by a young boy, the nephew of mathematician Edward Kasner, in the 1920s. The company name Google was inspired by it.

title: Pythagoras' theorem
body: In a right-angled triangle, a² + b² = c², where c is the hypotenuse. It gives distances on maps and screens, and the size of an AC impedance: |Z| = √(R² + X²). Over 300 different proofs are known.

title: Euclid: the primes never end
body: Suppose there were a largest prime. Multiply all the primes together and add 1. That number leaves remainder 1 when divided by every prime on the list, so it has a prime factor not on the list. Contradiction. Euclid proved it around 300 BC.

title: Why √2 is irrational
body: Assume √2 = p/q in lowest terms. Then p² = 2q², so p is even: p = 2k. Then 4k² = 2q², so q² = 2k² and q is even too. Both even contradicts 'lowest terms', so √2 cannot be a fraction. This is proof by contradiction.

title: The fundamental theorem of calculus
body: Differentiation and integration undo each other. To find the area under f(x) from a to b, find any F whose derivative is f and compute F(b) − F(a). Newton and Leibniz discovered it independently in the late 1600s.

title: The chain rule
body: To differentiate a function inside another, multiply the outer derivative by the inner one. d/dx sin(3x) = 3cos(3x), and d/dx (x² + 1)⁵ = 5(x² + 1)⁴ × 2x. It is the rule behind training neural networks (backpropagation).

title: Euler's identity
body: e^(iπ) + 1 = 0 links five key constants: e, i, π, 1 and 0. It comes from Euler's formula e^(iθ) = cos θ + i sin θ, which engineers use every day to turn sine waves into rotating phasors.

title: Taylor series
body: Smooth functions can be written as endless polynomials: eˣ = 1 + x + x²/2! + x³/3! + ... For small angles, sin θ ≈ θ (in radians). Calculators evaluate many functions this way, and engineers use these approximations constantly.

title: Bayes' theorem
body: P(A|B) = P(B|A) × P(A) ÷ P(B). If a disease affects 1 in 1,000 people and a test is 99% accurate both ways, a positive result means only about a 9% chance of disease: false positives among the 999 healthy people outnumber the true cases.

title: The central limit theorem
body: Add up many independent random effects and the total tends towards a normal (bell) curve, whatever the shape of each effect. That is why measurement errors, heights and electronic noise are so often normally distributed.

title: The law of large numbers
body: Repeat an experiment many times and the average result gets closer to the expected value. Ten coin tosses may give 7 heads; ten thousand will be very close to 50%. Insurers and casinos depend on it.

title: The pigeonhole principle
body: Put n + 1 items into n boxes and at least one box holds two. Simple but powerful: among 367 people, two must share a birthday; in a city of a million people, at least two have exactly the same number of hairs, since nobody has a million.

title: Logarithms: multiplying by adding
body: log(ab) = log a + log b. Before calculators, engineers multiplied with log tables and slide rules. Logs still measure things that span huge ranges: decibels, pH, earthquake magnitude and algorithm running times.

title: Fourier: every signal is sines
body: Joseph Fourier showed that any repeating signal can be built from sine waves at multiples of its basic frequency. A square wave is a sum of odd harmonics. Audio filters, MP3, JPEG and 4G radio all rely on Fourier analysis.

title: Fermat's Last Theorem
body: In 1637 Pierre de Fermat wrote that aⁿ + bⁿ = cⁿ has no whole-number solutions for n > 2, and that the margin was too small for his proof. Mathematicians failed to prove it for 358 years, until Andrew Wiles did in 1994.

title: Gödel's incompleteness theorems
body: In 1931 Kurt Gödel proved that any consistent set of rules rich enough to describe arithmetic contains true statements it cannot prove. No single list of axioms can capture all of mathematics.

title: The Riemann hypothesis
body: Proposed in 1859, it predicts where the zeros of the Riemann zeta function lie, which governs how prime numbers are spread out. It is a Millennium Prize Problem with a 1 million dollar reward, and it remains unsolved.

title: The four colour theorem
body: Any map can be coloured with just four colours so that no neighbouring regions match. Kenneth Appel and Wolfgang Haken proved it in 1976, the first major theorem proved with heavy help from a computer.

title: Derivative check
body: Calculus check.
explanation: Power rule: the derivative of xⁿ is n·xⁿ⁻¹, so x³ becomes 3x².

title: Integral check
body: Calculus check.
statement: The integral of 2x is x² + C
explanation: The derivative of x² is 2x, so integrating 2x gives x² plus a constant of integration C.

title: Is √2 a fraction?
body: Number theory check.
statement: √2 can be written as a fraction of two whole numbers
explanation: Assuming √2 = p/q in lowest terms forces both p and q to be even, a contradiction.

title: 0.999... and 1
body: Real numbers check.
explanation: Let x = 0.999... Then 10x = 9.999..., so 10x − x = 9, giving 9x = 9 and x = 1.

title: A logarithm
body: Logarithms check.
explanation: 10³ = 1000, so the base-10 logarithm of 1000 is 3.

title: A trig identity
body: Trigonometry check.
statement: sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 for every angle θ
explanation: It is Pythagoras' theorem on a circle of radius 1: the sides are cos θ and sin θ, the hypotenuse is 1.

title: Euler's identity check
body: Complex numbers check.
explanation: By Euler's formula, e^(iπ) = cos π + i sin π = −1, so adding 1 gives 0.
